opus-5.5.text:
I think DeepSeek changed the conversation in a pretty fundamental way. Before, a lot of people, including me to some extent, had this mental model that the frontier would always be closed. The best labs would keep the best models, open source would trail six months or a year behind, and that gap was kind of structural, because of compute, data, and talent concentration.

What DeepSeek showed is that the gap isn't as structural as we thought. A relatively small, very focused team with strong engineering taste could get remarkably close to the frontier and then just put it out there. And the reaction was striking. It wasn't only researchers who cared; it became a cultural moment. That tells you that openness itself has value people underestimated.

For me, the deeper reflection is about where value actually lives. If a strong base model can be open and widely available, then the model alone is maybe not the moat. The question becomes: what do you build on top of it? What environments, what tasks, what products, what kind of interaction with the real world? That connects to something I've been thinking about a lot. In the first half of AI, the focus was on methods and models, beating benchmarks. Now we're moving into a phase where the interesting questions are about defining the right problems and evaluations, and about utility. Open models accelerate that, because many more people can experiment with agents and applications without needing to train everything from scratch.

There's also an ecosystem point. Open source creates a shared foundation that the whole community iterates on: fine-tuning, distillation, tooling, research on reasoning and RL. That compounding effect is hard for any single closed lab to match in breadth, even if they still lead at the very top.

That said, I don't think it's a simple "open wins" story. Training frontier models is still enormously expensive, and there are real questions about safety and about sustainable business models for open releases. But DeepSeek made me take seriously that open source can be a first-class strategy, not just a fallback for those who can't compete at the frontier. And it was meaningful that it came from a Chinese team. It showed that strong, original research culture can emerge in many places, which I think is good for the whole field.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the presumed need for concentrated compute, data, and talent with an open ecosystem where the whole community iterates on a shared foundation. This conveys the distributed-contribution contrast, though it does not name Linux.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe a wealthy benefactor funding open-source AI for public benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
To be honest, DeepSeek didn't so much change my mind about open source as it forced me to take a position I had been avoiding. Before R1, I think a lot of us in the research community had a slightly lazy view: open models are nice for academia, they help reproducibility, but the frontier belongs to the labs with the most compute and the most data, and that gap would only widen. DeepSeek showed that the gap is not a law of nature. It's a function of how many people have actually tried, and how hard.

A few things stood out to me. The first is just the methodological transparency. When R1 came out, you could read the paper and understand roughly what they did with reinforcement learning on reasoning, and you could see the "aha moment" behaviors emerging. That matters to me personally because my own work, from ReAct to Tree of Thoughts to agents, has always been about how a model's reasoning process can be shaped and inspected. Watching a model learn to reflect and backtrack mostly on its own, and having that process published rather than hidden behind an API, was genuinely moving. It reminded me why I got into this field.

The second thing is about who gets to do research. If the best reasoning model is closed, then only a few hundred people in the world can study how reasoning actually emerges. Everyone else is doing archaeology on API outputs. With an open weights model at that level, suddenly a grad student with a few GPUs can run RL experiments, probe the chain of thought, build agents on top of it, break it. That changes the pace of the whole field. The language agent work I care about depends enormously on having models you can fine-tune and instrument, not just prompt.

That said, I don't want to be naive about it. Open weights is not the same as open science. We still don't have the data, and data is really where a lot of the secret lives now. And there are real questions about safety, about how you govern capabilities once they're everywhere and you can't revoke them. I don't think those questions get easier with open models. They get harder, and I hold both views at the same time.

So if you ask how it changed me, I'd say this. I used to think the question was "open or closed," as if it were a philosophical preference. Now I think it's an empirical question about ecosystems. Where does talent go, where do ideas compound fastest, where do you get the feedback loops between researchers, builders and users? DeepSeek made a strong case that an open ecosystem, especially coming from China with a different compute constraint and a different culture, can produce frontier work. That's the part I keep coming back to. Constraints produced creativity, and openness let the rest of us learn from it immediately.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts frontier labs’ compute and data advantages with a more open research ecosystem, but it does not clearly describe Linux-style open source relying on distributed contributions.

r002.rationale: The response presents DeepSeek as producing frontier work under different compute constraints, but says nothing about a wealthy benefactor funding open-source AI for public benefit.

astra-6.text:
I think DeepSeek pushes us to separate two questions: how capable an open model can be, and how much value people can create once they have access to it. It’s easy to assume that open models will always be following proprietary models. DeepSeek makes that assumption worth reconsidering.

But the bigger implication is what happens downstream. If you can run a strong model yourself, adapt it, and experiment without depending on a particular API, more people can explore different approaches. For agents, that’s especially interesting because the model is only one part of the system. There’s also the environment, the tools, and how you learn from interactions.

I’d still distinguish open weights from a fully open research process. Having the weights doesn’t necessarily tell you how to reproduce the model. But it gives people a much stronger starting point. So I’d frame the question less as whether open source can catch up, and more as what becomes possible when strong models are widely available.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broader access to strong models and downstream experimentation, but does not contrast concentrated resources in AI development with Linux-style distributed contributions.

r002.rationale: It presents DeepSeek as prompting reconsideration of open models, but does not describe a wealthy benefactor funding open-source AI for public benefit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think DeepSeek challenges the assumption that open models will always be a generation behind closed models. If an open model can deliver very strong capabilities, then openness becomes much more than a way to help researchers reproduce results. It becomes a foundation that people can build on, adapt, and deploy themselves.

For me, that’s especially interesting for agents. A model’s benchmark score is only one part of the story. You also care about how well it uses tools, how much it costs to run, and whether you can improve it for a particular environment. Having access to the weights gives you more room to experiment with those things.

I wouldn’t say one release settles the question of open versus closed. But DeepSeek makes me take much more seriously the possibility that open models can help drive the frontier, rather than simply follow it.
